chapters.title: A Warning About the Coming Meditations

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I want to give a little warning now, because tomorrow's meditation and the next one are a little more difficult. I'm not going to tell you what they are yet — I don't want to spoil it. But the idea is to look at the positive side of what's coming up. Our experience is full of great things that happened to us, and maybe some challenging things too. It's not about entertaining the story of something negative that happened to you — it's more an investigation into what seed was planted, and then you just go off on an imagination trip. What seed might have been planted that created the result you saw in your early life? So it's going to be fun.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So let's go for it. We're going to use the V Houses app. Brian used it yesterday during the meditation. And how do I know he used it? Because I follow Brian, and I know when he's meditating — a notification appeared on my phone that said, "Brian Mendoza is meditating. Want to join?" We're now in the localization process, helping each region translate this app, so it's going to be in everyone's language. Everyone's language will get their own version.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Get comfortable. So first, everyone comes to a comfortable position. That's how I get comfortable. It's an offering — especially if you're offering it to your partner, or the partner who isn't there yet that you're imagining will be there. Even if the partner isn't around yet, you can feed them in a similar way. Okay, anyway. Here we go. Close your eyes.

chapters.title: Guided Meditation — Meeting Your Future Self

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We're going to start with 100 breaths. Exhale first. Inhale, one. Exhale. Inhale, two. And continue on your own.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And now, seated in meditation: instead of inviting your teacher or somebody you admire, we're going to invite the future version of ourself — the most perfected version of ourselves we can imagine. Sit with your future you. Admire the qualities they have. What have they overcome? What have they let go of? See how they radiate the perfected qualities you're striving for. See them looking back at you, really happy — almost excited that you're on your way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then we're going to make an offering to our future self. Offer them your practice. Show them something you're doing that is going to directly help. And then let them know one thing you did recently that you're not so proud of — something you know goes against the thing you're trying to accomplish. Just let them know you did it. Maybe a moment of anger, or a moment of judgment. And then celebrate something you saw somebody else do — some goodness in somebody else.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Then ask them to give you teachings — to quickly teach you all the things you need to do to become like them. Ask them to come in unexpected ways, through other people. Then ask them to stay with you — to be with you, to keep inspiring and motivating you, and reminding you that you're much closer than you think. And then invite them to come into your heart — that they enter into your heart and stay there, always there as a resource to inspire you.

chapters.title: Guided Meditation — Childhood and the Senses

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And now we're going to look at our childhood. Today we're going to focus on certain things that appeared to us as children, and we're going to focus on our senses — things that really attracted you through touch, or through smell, or through sound. What kinds of things were you attracted to, or appeared in your world, that you were automatically attracted to for, quote, "no reason at all"?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, in my example: as a child, I had a little stuffed animal. Its little tiny feet were made of a slender, satin-soft fabric. As a child, I used to rub that fabric — that foot — between my fingers, very softly. I really enjoyed it. I can feel it even now as an adult. That feeling brought about a deep experience of safety and comfort. So, with that really strong feeling I remember from childhood — that feeling of safety and comfort — I go off on an imagination of what seeds were planted that created that experience for me. Logically, I know the seed must be similar to the result. So the ideas that came to me were: maybe I provided somebody with a really soft blanket when they were cold. Another idea: maybe I found a small animal outside — an abandoned cat — and wrapped it up and held it close to me, so it felt safe and warm. And another: basically being a mother to some kind of animal, taking care of their children. Maybe those seeds were created then, and ripened in this beautiful, soft stuffed animal that provided me safety and comfort.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So for the next fifteen minutes, go through things in your childhood that were really sensorily pleasurable or enjoyable, or created a great experience for you. Maybe it's something with touch. Maybe it's a smell. Maybe it's a song you heard. Maybe it's a taste. When you find one, just allow your mind to explore what could have caused that in a past life. What goodness caused it? Then, after you explore that, find another beautiful experience and explore that too. All right, continue on your own.
